Tapasya Fitness: Fifty-Two Minutes

Pune, the night of Sunday 13 September 2026. Three audiences need a number by Monday, and the three numbers available disagree with one another.

1. The night before

Meghna Saraf had turned off the lights in the study at half past eleven because the glare on the monitor was making it harder to think, and then turned them on again because she could not read the printouts spread across the floor. There were four of them, weighted at the corners with a stapler, a phone, a mug and a rolled-up yoga mat with the Tapasya logo peeling at the edge. Rain was coming down hard on Baner Road outside. The board met at half past nine the next morning at the company's office in Baner, with two directors joining from Mumbai and one from Singapore on video, and the second slide of the deck said, in 96-point type, 52.

Fifty-two was the company's weekly active minutes per subscriber for August 2026, up from 38 two years earlier. It was the number in the Series C pitch. It was the number in clause 7.3 of the contract with Tapasya's largest corporate customer in Dubai. It was the number thirty per cent of her own team's bonus pool was tied to. And it was, Meghna had concluded somewhere around eight that evening, a number she could no longer defend in a room where someone asked a hard question about it.

On the floor beside the board deck lay a two-page memo from Aparna Krishnan in Toronto, sent at 4:12 p.m. Pune time, subject line "Re: cohort tables for data room — read before Monday please". Beside that, a chart from Ritwik Sen's hardware telemetry showing completed workouts per subscriber falling for five consecutive quarters. Beside that, Lena Hoffmann's research deck from Berlin, fourteen moderated sessions in Nagpur and Kochi, with a slide titled "Nobody finishes setting up". And beside that, a WhatsApp thread from Grace Lim in Singapore that Meghna had not replied to, asking whether anything in the board deck was going to change what Tapasya reported to Dubai on the thirtieth.

She had until half past nine to decide what Tapasya Fitness would say it was measuring, and to whom.

2. How Tapasya got here

Tapasya Fitness was founded in Pune in 2019 by Kartik Bhalla, who had run growth at a food-delivery company, and Ritwik Sen, a mechanical engineer who had spent eleven years at an automotive supplier in Chakan. Their first product was the Tapasya One, a connected indoor cycle at ₹ 74,900 aimed at the urban household that had watched Peloton videos on Instagram. They sold 4,100 of them in eighteen months, mostly in Gurugram, Mumbai and Bengaluru, and learned two things: that the Indian market for a ₹ 75,000 piece of home exercise equipment was perhaps forty thousand households wide, and that servicing a heavy machine in a fourth-floor walk-up in Pune was a business nobody wanted to be in.

In 2022 they pivoted. The Tapasya Mat was a ₹ 12,999 yoga and strength mat with a grid of pressure sensors, a Bluetooth module, and a companion app that counted repetitions, corrected posture by inference, and streamed live classes in English, Hindi, Marathi and Tamil. Subscription was ₹ 499 a month for Tapasya Live. By FY26 the company had sold 2.8 lakh mats cumulatively, had 1.14 lakh paying subscribers, and had booked ₹ 218 crore of revenue — ₹ 131 crore hardware, ₹ 61 crore subscription, ₹ 26 crore from a corporate wellness business that had grown almost by accident after a Bengaluru technology services firm bought 900 seats in 2023.

The decision that constrained everything Meghna could now do had been taken in the funding winter of 2023, and it had been taken for good reasons. Cash was tight, the analytics bill was ₹ 41 lakh a quarter, and Kartik wanted it halved. The company moved to a cheaper event pipeline with ninety-day raw-event retention, dropped device-attribute enrichment on Android versions below 11 to cut volume, and sampled non-critical events at twenty per cent. In the same quarter, in the same board meeting, Weekly Active Minutes per subscriber — WAM — was adopted as the single company objective, and the compensation committee tied thirty per cent of the product, growth and engineering bonus pool to it. The comp plan was locked until 31 March 2027.

Three years later, the consequences had compounded quietly. Tapasya could not build a clean cohort older than ninety days without reconstructing it from aggregated daily snapshots. It could not reliably tell what had happened on the phones of the roughly thirty-eight per cent of its base still on older Android builds. And it had an organisation in which asking whether WAM was the right metric was, for about two hundred people, a question about their own bonus.

3. The industry around it

The at-home fitness market in India in 2026 was crowded at the edges and thin in the middle. Cult.fit had built the dominant branded gym network and pushed its at-home app aggressively; Decathlon sold unconnected equipment at a quarter of Tapasya's price in 96 Indian stores; boAt and Noise had put a wearable on tens of millions of wrists at ₹ 1,500 to ₹ 4,000, normalising the idea of a daily activity number while setting expectations about what such data was worth paying for; Garmin and Apple owned the premium wrist. HealthifyMe and a dozen smaller apps owned nutrition coaching. Distribution ran through Amazon and Flipkart for the bulk of retail volume, with Reliance Retail's electronics format carrying the mat in 140 stores from the 2025 festive season, and Jio bundling three months of Tapasya Live with certain fibre plans in a partnership that had brought 61,000 trials and 4,900 conversions.

Three regulatory facts shaped the product directly. First, the mat's electronics required registration under the Bureau of Indian Standards' compulsory registration scheme, and Ritwik's sensor revision 3 — the one that would fix the pressure-drift problem — needed eleven weeks of re-certification before a single unit could ship. Second, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed everything Tapasya collected: heart rate captured through the paired wearable was collected under a consent notice that specified use for "personalised class recommendations and your own progress reports", which Tapasya's counsel had advised did not extend to aggregate reporting to a corporate customer's human resources department without fresh, purpose-specific consent. Third, the Reserve Bank of India's rules on recurring e-mandates — additional factor authentication and a pre-debit notification for subscription auto-debits — had, when enforced more strictly in 2024, produced a churn spike of 2.9 percentage points in a single month that the company had spent a year recovering from and that still distorted every retention series that crossed it.

Globally, Tapasya's exposure was small but disproportionate in influence. Fourteen corporate accounts, of which the largest was Marhaba Infra Group in Dubai: 4,200 enrolled employees, ₹ 9.6 crore of annual recurring revenue, and a contract up for renewal on 31 December 2026 whose clause 7.3 put twelve per cent of the fee at risk if "average weekly engagement minutes per enrolled employee" fell below 45. Nikhil Prabhu, hired in New Jersey in 2025, was chasing United States employers who asked about clinical outcomes rather than minutes. And the lead investor for the Series C — ₹ 340 crore at a ₹ 2,100 crore pre-money valuation — was a Singapore fund whose diligence list, received on 28 August, asked for "monthly cohort retention and completed-session data by acquisition channel, 24 months".

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The sequence mattered, because at each point the company had believed something that later proved not to hold.

Exhibit 1 · Timeline of belief and revision

The uncomfortable feature of Exhibit 1 is that the two rows which explain most of the recent rise in the company's headline metric — the lobby autoplay and the notification programme — were both shipped by teams whose bonus depended on that metric rising, and neither was shipped with any intent to game it. Both were reasonable product decisions. Both had the side effect of making the number move without making the product better at the thing it was sold to do.

5. The people

Meghna Saraf, chief product officer, Pune. Joined in 2024 from a payments company. Her stated position is that Tapasya cannot enter a Series C data room with a metric it cannot explain, and that the board should be told before the investor discovers it. Her incentive is complicated: her own bonus is tied to WAM, and she has been at the company fourteen months, which is short enough that a metric controversy she creates will be read as her judgement about her predecessors. What she is not saying is that she has not read Aparna's memo closely enough to know whether the shadow pipeline Aparna built without approval would itself survive investor diligence.

Kartik Bhalla, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai four days a week. Position: hold the line on WAM for FY27, footnote the definition changes, and revisit after the round closes. Incentive: the round includes a secondary component, and a metric controversy in September costs him both valuation and time. What he is not saying is that the Singapore fund's associate had already asked him, on a call on 4 September, for completed-session data, and that he had said it would come with the rest of the data-room material.

Ritwik Sen, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune. Position: the mat's sensors are the only honest witness; app minutes are a marketing number. Incentive: revision 3 needs ₹ 2.4 crore of tooling and eleven weeks of BIS re-certification, and a public argument about measurement error strengthens his case for the budget. What he is not saying is that the drift defect he found in July also means his own five-quarter decline in completions is partly an artefact of ageing hardware rather than declining use, and he does not yet know how much.

Dr Sunita Iyengar, vice-president of growth, Bengaluru. Position: WAM is the only metric with three years of continuous history, the company has no business changing its objective nine weeks before a fundraise, and every alternative on the table has worse data behind it. Incentive: thirty per cent of a bonus pool covering 38 people in her organisation, locked until 31 March 2027. What she is not saying is that she knows how much of the FY26 gain came from lobby autoplay, because her analyst ran that decomposition in June and did not circulate it.

Lena Hoffmann, principal designer, Berlin. Position: the company is measuring the wrong layer entirely; the defect is that a first-time user cannot get from an unboxed mat to a finished class, and that is measurable if anyone chooses to measure it. Incentive: a research function of one, asking for three more people and ₹ 1.1 crore. What she is not saying is that her fourteen participants were recruited through a panel vendor and skewed towards English-speaking households with home broadband, which is not the base — and that she declined to run the study in Bhopal because the vendor's quote was ₹ 6 lakh higher.

Aparna Krishnan, staff data scientist, Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Pune. Position: no metric decision should be taken before the pipeline is rebuilt, because sampling at twenty per cent and ninety-day retention make every cohort claim in the deck an estimate presented as a fact. Incentive: she wrote a memo in 2023 opposing the pipeline downgrade, was overruled, and has kept the memo. What she is not saying is that she has spent four months of her own time building a parallel event store on infrastructure she provisioned without a budget line, that it reconstructs only back to March 2026, and that its numbers disagree with the official ones by between four and eleven per cent depending on the metric.

Grace Lim, customer success lead, Singapore. Position: report exactly what clause 7.3 says, change nothing before 31 December, and do not give Marhaba a reason to reopen the contract. Incentive: her variable compensation is tied to the ₹ 9.6 crore renewal. What she is not saying is the content of the 6 September call: Marhaba's head of people, Zayan Qureshi, told her that his own board was sceptical of minutes and would find "sessions finished" more credible — and Grace suspects that on a completions basis Marhaba's fleet would look considerably worse than 45 minutes a week looks now.

Nikhil Prabhu, head of sales, New Jersey. Position: minutes are unsellable in the United States market, where employer buyers and their benefits consultants ask about adherence and health outcomes; Tapasya needs a completion and outcome metric to compete there at all. Incentive: a $4.1 million pipeline and a commission plan that pays on new logos. What he is not saying is that he has already shown two prospects a slide with completion figures he pulled himself from Ritwik's hardware dashboard, unreviewed, and that one of those prospects has quoted the figure back to him in writing.

7. Voices

Kartik Bhalla, WhatsApp to Meghna, 11 September, 10:47 p.m.Meghna I hear you on the footnotes. But understand the sequencing. We close in November. Every single company in this sector reports engagement minutes. If we invent a new metric in September the first question is why, and the second question is what were you hiding. Put the caveats in the appendix. We fix the instrument in Q4 with the new money.
Aparna Krishnan, memo to Meghna, 13 September, 4:12 p.m.I want to be precise about what I am and am not saying. I am not saying WAM is fake. I am saying we cannot compute a 24-month cohort series at all, and that the series in the deck is stitched from daily aggregates whose definitions changed twice. When I rebuild August from raw events in the parallel store, I get 47.6, not 52.0 — the gap is lobby time and the paused-account denominator. I cannot tell you which is right because the official number is not wrong by its own definition. That is the problem. A number that cannot be wrong cannot be evidence.
Sunita Iyengar, product review, Bengaluru, 9 SeptemberCan I say the unfashionable thing? Three years ago this company had eleven dashboards and no direction. One metric fixed that. Now we have a bad quarter on hardware telemetry — telemetry that Ritwik himself says is broken on a fifth of the fleet — and suddenly the metric is the villain. If we change the objective now, I have thirty-eight people whose bonus arithmetic stops making sense in October and I will lose four of them by December. Tell me which four you want me to lose.
Lena Hoffmann, Slack #product-leads, 10 September, 7:02 p.m. ISTFourteen people. Nine could not pair the mat without help. Two thought the hardware was broken. I know fourteen is not a sample. But look at Exhibit 7 — thirty-one per cent finish one class. Whatever number we put on the board slide, the honest description of this product today is that two-thirds of the people who paid ₹ 12,999 never once did the thing they bought it for. Which of our five dashboards says that?
Ritwik Sen, reply, 10 September, 7:31 p.m. ISTLena is right about the conclusion and wrong about the evidence. Exhibit 7's missing row is a pairing failure and I can tell you it is mostly BLE on old Androids and mostly fixable in firmware, not design. But I want it on record that the mat has been telling us completions are falling for five quarters and nobody looked, because nobody's bonus was attached to it.
Grace Lim, email to Meghna, 12 September, 8:15 a.m. SGTPlease confirm nothing changes in the monthly report before 31 Dec. Clause 7.3 is minutes. If we start sending Zayan a completions figure now, we are renegotiating from a position we have not analysed. I will say separately that he raised it himself on the 6th and I did not encourage it.
Nikhil Prabhu, Slack DM to Meghna, 12 September, 9:40 p.m. ISTI have a benefits consultant in Hartford asking for adherence data by Friday. Minutes mean nothing to her. I used Ritwik's completions number in a deck last month because it was the only thing that answered the question. If we are going to have an official version of that number I would like to know before my customer does.

8. The options as Meghna sees them

By midnight she had four written on the back of the board agenda, and an uneasy sense that the list itself was the wrong list.

One: hold WAM for FY27. Present 52, add an appendix restating the definition changes and the denominator, commit to a measurement review in Q4. Keeps the round, the comp plan and the Dubai contract undisturbed. Costs nothing this quarter. Accepts that the data room will contain a series the company's own senior data scientist will not vouch for, and that the Singapore fund has already asked for the thing that would contradict it.

Two: freeze and rebuild. Put two engineers and ₹ 1.1 crore on rebuilding the event pipeline — full retention, no sampling, pairing instrumented on old Androids — and refuse to commit to any new objective for ten weeks. Aparna's position, and unanswerable on the merits. It also means going into the board meeting with no metric at all, arriving at the data-room deadline of 1 October with a rebuild in progress, and telling Nikhil to wait until December.

Three: publish the fuller picture now, warts included. Take five measures to the board — completions per subscriber, first-class completion rate, retail satisfaction by language, paused-account share, and WAM as a monitored guardrail with no target — and say plainly that three of the five look bad and two are poorly instrumented. Buys credibility and a mandate. Risks a round at a lower valuation, a growth organisation whose bonus basis has evaporated in month six of a locked plan, and a Dubai renewal conversation opened on Tapasya's initiative rather than the customer's.

Four: split the measurement by business. Retail is measured on first-class completion and second-week return; corporate is measured on enrolled-employee adherence as the contract defines it; the company reports both and stops pretending one number describes both. Honest about a real structural difference. It also doubles the reporting burden, gives Sunita's team two targets instead of one, requires fresh DPDP consent for anything that aggregates health data for a corporate customer, and quietly concedes that Tapasya has been running two products with one dashboard for three years.

What kept troubling her, in the version of the argument she rehearsed at one in the morning, was that all four options were answers to the question "what number should we report?" None of them answered the questions she could not stop reformulating: which decision, exactly, needs a number by Monday, and which needs one by December, and are they the same number? Who would own each measure once it existed, and at what cadence would anyone look? And if 31 per cent of buyers never complete a class, is the problem that Tapasya is measuring the wrong thing, or that it has known the wrong thing for five quarters and no one whose bonus depended on it had any reason to look?

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Board meeting, 14 September, 9:30 a.m. IST. Series C data room to be populated by 1 October; the Singapore fund's diligence list requires 24 months of cohort and completed-session data. Marhaba renewal 31 December, clause 7.3 minutes-based with twelve per cent of ₹ 9.6 crore at risk, and Zayan Qureshi's next quarterly review on 14 October. Compensation plan, with thirty per cent of a 200-person bonus pool on WAM, locked until 31 March 2027; the board's compensation committee meets next in January. Product budget for the quarter: ₹ 4.2 crore, of which ₹ 2.4 crore is already committed to sensor revision 3 tooling, which in turn needs eleven weeks of BIS re-certification before shipping. Two engineers uncommitted, in Pune, from 1 October. Legal advice on file that aggregate health reporting to a corporate customer requires fresh purpose-specific consent under the DPDP Act, which would have to be collected from 4,200 Marhaba employees through their employer, in Dubai, under a contract that does not contemplate it. Lena's research function is one person. Aparna's parallel event store reaches back to March 2026 and is not on any approved infrastructure list.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibits 3 and 4 describe the same product and move in opposite directions. Working only from the footnotes, list the specific adjustments you would need to make to each series before they could be compared, and say which adjustments the case gives you enough information to make.

2. Exhibit 6 reports a satisfaction score of +48 for Dubai and +2 for Hindi and Marathi retail users. What is that gap actually measuring? What would you have to do differently to find out?

3. Exhibit 7 leaves a row blank rather than estimating it. Aparna calls it the most important row in the table. Do you agree, and what would you be willing to conclude from the rows around it in the meantime?

4. Sunita argues that changing the objective destroys a compensation basis for 200 people six months into a locked plan. Is that an argument about measurement or about governance, and what does your answer imply about who should own the choice of a company's product metrics?

5. Each of the eight people in Section 5 is withholding something. Pick the three withholdings you judge most consequential for Meghna's decision, and explain how the decision changes if each comes to light on Tuesday instead of in November.

6. It is 9:30 on Monday morning. What does Meghna do — not in the abstract, but in the sequence of the next five working days — and what exactly does she say to the board about the number on slide two? If she says less than the whole of what she now believes, on what basis is that defensible?

At ten past one she stacked the four printouts, put the mug in the sink, and opened the board deck one last time. Slide two still said 52. She typed a footnote under it — "definition revised Nov 2024 and Mar 2026; see appendix" — read it twice, and deleted it, because a footnote that small either meant nothing or meant everything, and she did not yet know which one she intended. Outside, the rain had thinned to the sound of water running off the terrace. In Toronto it was quarter to four in the afternoon and Aparna was online. In Berlin, Lena had sent one more message with fourteen photographs attached. Meghna left the laptop open on the table, switched off the study light, and stood for a while in the doorway without deciding anything at all.

UX Metrics and the HEART Framework: Measuring the Experience Itself

A framework that is easy to recite and hard to run. What separates the teams that get decisions out of HEART from the teams that get dashboards.

Section 1Two rooms, one week apart

On 4 February 2026, in a converted mill building in Pune, Shruti Kamath sat with a rollout decision she had postponed for three weeks. She is VP Product at Vistrit Care Cloud, which sells clinical documentation software to forty-one hospital groups across India, covering roughly 19,000 licensed beds. Her team had rebuilt the discharge summary composer — the screen on which a resident assembles a patient's discharge note before a consultant signs it. The pilot data were, on their face, bad: across ten pilot sites, the share of summaries completed in a single sitting without abandoning the draft had fallen from 67.6% on the old composer to 58.4% on the new one. Her engineering director wanted to roll back. Her design lead wanted to ship. Both were reading the same number.

Eight days later and 840 kilometres south, Nandita Bhargava faced a different trouble. She is co-founder and chief product officer of Wistaan Studio, a Bengaluru company whose product drafts catalogue listings and customer replies for about 34,000 small online sellers, most of them one- or two-person operations. Wistaan's weekly numbers had never looked better: drafts per seller up 31% quarter on quarter, in-product satisfaction at 4.3 out of 5, and the share of drafts accepted without any editing up from 26% to 34%. Yet the metric the company was funded on — the share of listings that sold within fourteen days of publication — had drifted down 2.6 points over the same period. Her data lead, Imran Qureshi, put it plainly in the Monday review: every experience metric we own improved, and the seller is worse off.

These two rooms frame the argument of this page. Shruti's problem is that an experience metric can be true and still be misread; Nandita's is that one can be improved and still be wrong. HEART is what most teams reach for in both situations, and in both, reciting the five letters does nothing. What does something is the discipline underneath them, and knowing the conditions under which it breaks.

Section 2The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

HEART is a taxonomy of user-experience metric categories — Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success — paired with a selection procedure, Goals–Signals–Metrics, that forces a team to state what should be true before naming a number. Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson and Xin Fu, then at Google, published it in 2010 in a CHI paper whose title named the real problem: measuring user experience on a large scale. Small-scale usability research already had rigorous instruments; what did not exist was a way to carry those constructs into a telemetry pipeline, in a vocabulary product teams would adopt.

The lineage tells you what HEART is entitled to claim. Three strands converge. The usability tradition codified in ISO 9241-11 defines usability as effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use — the first two become Task Success, the third Happiness. The psychometric survey tradition, from the System Usability Scale (1986) onward, established that attitudes toward software can be measured with acceptable reliability if the instrument is held constant. The third strand, which Rodden wrote against, is the operational-metrics culture summarised as PULSE — page views, uptime, latency, seven-day actives, earnings — indispensable and nearly useless for product decisions: lagging, dominated by traffic and marketing, and capable of staying flat for two quarters after a redesign ruins a core task.

The schools that disagree about HEART are best separated by the propositions each will and will not sign. The behaviouralist school signs "attitudinal metrics may inform, but must never be a team's primary decision metric," citing response rates in low single digits and the weak predictive validity of stated satisfaction for churn. It will not sign "attitudes are noise": logs cannot see intention. The perceived-quality school, from HCI research, signs the reverse: "under switching costs, behaviour measures captivity, not quality," pointing at enterprise software with 100% weekly usage and a net promoter score of 8. It will not sign "surveys can replace telemetry."

A third position, from the North Star lineage, signs "five categories times a Goals–Signals–Metrics table per surface costs more attention than it returns; pick one metric and three inputs." A fourth, the critique most worth taking seriously, signs: "HEART is a taxonomy, not a theory — it says what kinds of things can be measured, not which one matters here, and contains no causal model connecting experience to outcome." That critique is correct, and the rest of this page is about what practitioners put in the gap it names.

Section 3Mechanics in depth: what experts actually do between "pick a category" and "read the dashboard"

The published procedure is short: choose categories, write a Goal, derive a Signal, define a Metric. Expert practice inserts four steps the paper leaves implicit, and these determine whether the resulting number ever changes a decision.

The first is scoping the unit of analysis. "Task success rate" is ambiguous until you say whether the denominator is users, sessions or attempts. A resident who abandons a draft four times in a shift contributes four failures at attempt level, one at session level, and possibly a success at user level if the fifth attempt worked. Attempt-level ratios carry a further trap: when the analysis unit is finer than the randomisation unit, naive variance is understated and teams declare significance that is not there. The corrections — the delta method, or a bootstrap resampling users rather than attempts — typically widen the interval by 1.5 to 2.5 times.

The second is choosing a statistic, not just a metric. Vistrit's redesign moved median composition time from 7 minutes 40 seconds to 4 minutes 50 seconds, a 37% improvement the design lead quoted in every meeting. The 95th percentile moved the other way: 22 minutes to 27 minutes. The new composer was faster for routine cases and slower for complex ones, because it front-loaded a structured template that multi-comorbidity patients kept overflowing. A mean hides both facts; only the distribution shows the trade the team actually made.

The third is the sensitivity check, which most cleanly separates a decision metric from a reporting metric: before adopting a metric, compute the minimum detectable effect at the sample size the team will actually have. For a proportion near p = 0.64, detecting a 3-point change at 80% power and 5% significance needs roughly 16 × p(1−p) / δ² = 16 × 0.230 / 0.0009 ≈ 4,100 units per arm. Vistrit sees about 9,000 discharge summaries a week across pilot sites, so a task-success metric can decide something inside a fortnight. Its Happiness metric cannot: at a 4.8% response rate the team collects about 430 responses a week, and the standard error on a 62% favourable rate is √(0.62 × 0.38 / 430) = 2.34pp, giving roughly ±4.6 points at 95%. A five-point change in satisfaction is invisible. That is not an argument against measuring Happiness, but for measuring it quarterly with a fixed instrument and refusing to explain weekly wobbles.

The fourth is pairing every metric with a counter-metric. Any HEART metric can be moved by degrading something outside its frame: Task Success rises if you narrow the task, Engagement if you make the product harder to use, Adoption if you nag. Expert practice writes the guardrail into the same row as the metric, with a stated tolerance, not onto a health dashboard nobody reads during a launch.

Section 4When the framework applies, and when it actively misleads

Three conditions can be stated as testable claims, each resolving differently for the two protagonists. Claim one: the surface has a definable task with an observable completion event. Vistrit passes cleanly — a summary is either submitted or not. Wistaan fails: a generated draft has no natural completion event, because the seller may accept it, edit it heavily, or copy it into a channel Wistaan cannot see. Where completion is unobservable, Task Success metrics silently become acceptance metrics, which measure something else entirely.

Claim two: the user has a live alternative. This governs whether Happiness and Retention carry information. A resident cannot choose a different composer; her satisfaction score measures endurance and her retention measures employment. Wistaan's sellers can abandon the product between two cups of tea, so their retention curve is a genuine quality signal. Where there is no alternative, Happiness must be re-anchored to something the user can withhold — discretionary use, voluntary feature adoption, willingness to recommend to a peer at another hospital.

Claim three: the measured experience is causally upstream of the outcome the business needs. This is where HEART most often misleads, and where Nandita's problem sits. Wistaan's acceptance rate is upstream of nothing except itself: a model tuned to produce drafts sellers accept verbatim produces safe, generic listings, and generic listings sell less. Whenever an experience metric can be optimised by making the product blander, HEART without a downstream link is a machine for confident wrong decisions.

Section 5Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Two-sided markets. Vartul Market, a home-services marketplace in six Indian cities, found one HEART set structurally incapable of describing it. Task Success for a customer is "a verified professional confirmed within ten minutes"; for the professional it is "a job worth the travel." Raising the first by auto-assigning jobs lowered the second: acceptance-to-completion fell from 91% to 84% as professionals took jobs they later dropped. Mature marketplaces run parallel tables plus a joint one for the transaction, and treat any metric moving in opposite directions across sides as a design constraint, not a reporting problem.

Regulated products. Vistrit cannot define Task Success as speed alone: a discharge summary is a legal record with statutory content requirements, so success carries a correctness term only a consultant's sign-off supplies, hours later and unattributable to a session. Regulated teams accept a two-clock system — a fast proxy for iteration, a slow verified metric for quarterly truth — and check periodically that the two have not decoupled.

Hardware plus software. Warsha Water Systems sells connected purifiers with a companion app. After a 2025 firmware release, weekly app sessions per device rose from 1.8 to 4.3 and the growth team celebrated a 139% Engagement gain. Service calls per thousand devices rose from 21 to 38 in the same window, and relationship NPS fell fourteen points over two quarters. The engagement was anxiety: a miscalibrated filter-life sensor had customers checking repeatedly. For a companion app to a physical good, Engagement is usually a metric to be minimised, guarded by an alert-resolution term.

AI-native products. Wistaan's category. Output is non-deterministic, so the same user doing the same task twice may succeed once; success becomes a distribution over outputs. Mature AI teams measure at three levels — output quality against a held-out rubric, interaction success (did the user reach something usable, at what editing cost), and downstream value — and never let the middle level stand alone.

The organisational seam. In most companies Happiness belongs to research, Engagement, Adoption and Retention to analytics, and Task Success to nobody, since it needs a funnel definition spanning both. What mature companies do, as opposed to what their charters say, is assign Task Success to the product manager personally — the only category whose definition is a product judgement rather than a measurement craft.

Section 6The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. The direction of goodness is a property of the job, not of the metric

A competent practitioner treats Engagement as something to increase; an expert asks first what the surface is for. Warsha's app, a password reset flow and an insurance claim form all want less engagement. The tell is a team reporting "sessions up" for a surface users visit only when something has gone wrong: the obvious reading inverts precisely where the product exists to eliminate a problem.

2. Attitudinal numbers move when the instrument moves

Changing a prompt from a post-task modal to a store rating request, or a five-point scale to an agreement statement, shifts the score more than most product changes do. The tell is a step change in Happiness with no behavioural counterpart and a release note mentioning the survey. Experts freeze the instrument and treat any change to it as a break in the series, annotated on the chart, not as news.

3. Segment mix moves aggregate rates without any user's experience changing

This is Shruti's actual problem. The new composer was better at every kind of site and worse in total, because the rollout order loaded small nursing homes — harder cases, less training — into the new arm. The tell is an aggregate that contradicts every segment; the diagnostic is to recompute it holding segment mix fixed.

4. Adoption is only a real category when there is a moment of choice

Measuring Adoption of a default-on feature produces a number describing the rollout schedule, not the user; the tell is an adoption curve that traces the release ramp exactly. Where there is no opt-in moment, experts substitute sustained discretionary use — the share who return in a later week without being routed there — which reintroduces the choice the default removed.

5. Retention without a triggering event measures the product, not the feature

"Week-four retention of Smart Feature users" usually means retention of people active enough to see it, which restates overall retention. The tell is a feature curve sitting a constant few points above the product curve, in parallel. Experts cohort on a triggering action and compare against a matched control of users who did not trigger it.

6. A metric that cannot detect the change you plan to make is decoration

The sensitivity arithmetic in Section 3 determines review cadence. A metric with a 4.6-point margin of error reviewed weekly generates eight explanations a quarter for noise, and that organisational cost is real. The tell is a recurring agenda item where the discussion is always about why a number wobbled.

7. Happiness and Retention diverge informatively, not contradictorily

Satisfied users leave and dissatisfied users stay, routinely, and each pattern names a condition: the first is usually low ongoing need or a solved problem, the second is switching cost. The tell is a team reconciling the two as if one must be wrong. Experts plot them by cohort and read the quadrant, because the quadrant is the finding.

8. The task in Task Success must be the user's task, not the screen's

Wistaan measures "draft accepted" at 34%; the seller's task is not to accept a draft but to sell an item, and every narrowing inflates the number while deflating its meaning. The tell is a success rate improving steadily while support volume and downstream conversion do not move. The diagnostic is to ask what the user would say they came to do, in their own words, then check whether the metric would register failure if that did not happen.

9. Aggregation across surfaces destroys the signal HEART exists to create

A company-level scorecard averages a healthy onboarding flow with a failing settlement flow and reports mild health. The tell is a scorecard whose numbers never move; the granularity that would move them has been averaged away. HEART is a per-surface instrument, and the right number of scorecards is roughly the number of jobs the product does.

Section 7How the practice differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the practice is close to the framework as written: large samples make every category measurable, and the constraint is choosing few enough metrics to act on. In B2B and enterprise, three things change. Buyer and user differ, so Adoption is measured per seat within an account and Happiness at both levels — the administrator who renews and the clerk who suffers. Samples are small enough that attitudinal metrics stop being weekly instruments. And retention is contractual, so the informative variant is usage retention within retained accounts, the leading indicator that a renewal conversation will go badly.

For platforms and marketplaces no single HEART set is valid, as Vartul found; the framework is instantiated per role, with the transaction measured separately. For hardware, the inversion of Engagement is the main structural difference, together with the fact that the experience includes events — installation, filter replacement, a service visit — that no app telemetry sees, so the system must join field service records to product analytics or it measures a shadow.

For AI products the difference is genuine: the mapping from intent to behaviour is stochastic, so a metric must be defined over a distribution of outcomes, and the editing cost a user pays to repair an output becomes a first-class Task Success statistic in a way it never was for deterministic software. Where the difference is not real, and where current writing overclaims: Adoption and Retention behave exactly as they always did, and inventing new categories for AI products mostly produces vocabulary.

By stage the honest summary is short. Pre-product-market-fit, samples are too small for stable retention curves or survey precision; the useful categories are Task Success measured almost qualitatively and Happiness gathered through conversation. At scale, Retention and Engagement carry the weight and the problem becomes governance — who owns which metric, at what cadence, informing which decision. That question, not the choice of categories, separates a mature measurement programme from a mature-looking one.

Section 8Three worked examples, including one that failed

Example one: Vistrit resolves the contradiction

Rohan Deshpande, Shruti's analyst, re-ran the pilot with segment mix held fixed, producing the 71.6% figure in Table 2, then checked the guardrails. Consultant edit rate had risen from 18.4% to 19.1%, inside the 3-point tolerance; p95 composition time had breached its guardrail, a 23% worsening against a 10% limit. The decision was therefore neither "ship" nor "roll back" but a third option the aggregate had hidden: ship to teaching hospitals, hold small nursing homes until the template overflow path for multi-comorbidity cases is fixed. The mix-adjusted number changed the verdict; the guardrail changed the scope.

Example two: Wistaan finds the downstream link

Imran Qureshi split one week's 12,400 drafts three ways and joined each to a fourteen-day sales outcome.

Wistaan redefined Task Success as "draft published and sold within fourteen days" and accepted a headline number that would look worse for two quarters.

Example three: Warsha, and what recovery cost

Warsha's failure was not the miscalibrated sensor but that the measurement system had no way to register the sensor as a problem. Engagement was sessions per device per week with no guardrail, Happiness was app store rating (dominated by prompt timing), and service call data sat in a separate system owned by operations. For eleven weeks a rising number was read as a win. The cost of catching it late was concrete: roughly 4,900 unnecessary service visits at a fully loaded ₹640 each, about ₹31 lakh, plus a fourteen-point NPS decline that took three quarters to recover.

The recovery is more interesting than the failure. Warsha did not add metrics; it changed signs and joined systems. Engagement got a declining target and an alert-resolution guardrail. It introduced a composite it called silent success — the share of device-weeks with zero app sessions, zero alerts and zero service events — which stood at 61% and reached 84% eleven months later. And it made the product manager, not operations, the owner of service call rate, on the argument that a service call is an experience failure that happens to be resolved by a van.

Section 9Failure modes, their early warning signs, and the cost of catching them late

Metric-first selection. The team adopts whatever is already instrumented and writes the goal afterwards. Early sign: nobody can state a metric's Goal and Signal from memory. Diagnostic: what would we do differently if this number moved five points? Caught late, a quarter of roadmap has been justified by a number that never measured the thing.

Unowned metrics. A scorecard with no named owner or cadence decays into decoration within two quarters. Early sign: charts narrated in reviews but never acted on. Diagnostic: for each metric, who is accountable, reviewed how often, deciding what?

Goodhart drift. Once a team is measured on Task Success, the definition of "task" narrows. Early sign: the metric improves faster than any qualitative signal. Diagnostic: re-derive the metric from its written Goal and ask whether the current definition still follows. Caught late, a year has been spent optimising a definition.

Unjoined systems. Warsha's mode: the data that would falsify the happy reading sits in another department's warehouse. Early sign: experience metrics and service volumes tell different stories and nobody owns the reconciliation. The cost shows up in operating expense and brand, as ₹31 lakh did.

Precision theatre. Reporting satisfaction to one decimal place weekly on 430 responses. Early sign: recurring explanations of movements smaller than the confidence interval. The cost is credibility — a leadership team that learns these numbers wobble meaninglessly discounts the ones that matter.

Section 10Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is whether attitudinal metrics belong in a product team's decision set at all. The behaviouralist case at its strongest: respondents are a self-selected 3–5% with systematically different motivation, stated satisfaction correlates weakly with subsequent behaviour, and under switching costs it measures resignation. Its evidence is the documented gap between stated intent and revealed preference. It would be wrong if attitudes predicted behaviours logs cannot see — word-of-mouth, procurement advocacy, tolerance of a future failure — and there is real evidence they do, particularly in B2B renewals. The perceived-quality case is exactly that: a product surviving on captivity accumulates a liability no behavioural metric shows until a competitor arrives.

The second is breadth versus focus. The North Star position holds that five categories multiplied across surfaces produce more measurement than any organisation can act on, and that one metric with three inputs concentrates attention; its evidence is organisational. The HEART-as-written reply is that a single metric always hides a trade — engagement bought with anxiety, success bought by narrowing the task — and the categories exist to make trades visible. It would be wrong if guardrails on one metric caught the same trades, which in Warsha's case they would have, had any existed.

The third, least settled, is whether Task Success can be defined at all for generative products. One camp holds that with a rubric, a held-out evaluation set and an editing-cost measure, success is measurable, just noisily. The other holds that when intent is formed by what the system offers, success is not well defined — the user had no task before the draft appeared. Nandita's team lives inside this disagreement: their sellers often could not have specified the listing they eventually published. Nobody has a clean answer, and a page offering one would mislead.

Section 11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied HEART can name the categories and produce a Goals–Signals–Metrics table on request. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. They argue about the denominator before the number, because the unit of analysis decides what a metric can mean. They ask for the distribution rather than the average, and treat a tail that moved the wrong way as a finding, not an outlier. They refuse a metric until they know its minimum detectable effect at the sample size the team actually has, and set review cadence from that arithmetic rather than the calendar. And they write the guardrail in the same breath as the metric, having seen every category gamed and knowing which way each drifts.

One further habit is diagnostic: an expert treats a contradiction between two HEART categories as the most valuable thing on the dashboard and goes to it first, where a competent practitioner reconciles it into a single narrative for the review.

Section 12The decisions, and three questions

Shruti Kamath shipped the new composer to teaching hospitals on 20 February and held the nursing-home cohort for six weeks pending a fix to the complex-case path. Her reasoning: the aggregate was an artefact of rollout order, the mix-adjusted four-point gain was real and within the edit-rate tolerance, and the breached p95 guardrail identified a specific fixable population rather than a reason to abandon the design. She also stratified future rollouts by site type, so a mix shift could never again masquerade as a product effect.

Nandita Bhargava made the harder decision. Wistaan retired verbatim acceptance as a headline metric for a fourteen-day sale-through rate on published listings, knowing the replacement is slower, noisier, and would make the product look worse in the next board pack. Her reasoning was that the old metric was optimisable in a direction that hurt sellers, and a team measured on an easily gamed proxy will eventually game it without ever deciding to. Edit distance and satisfaction stayed as diagnostics with no targets attached.

For discussion: (1) Vistrit's residents cannot choose another composer. What should Happiness concretely measure when users are captive, and how would you know your answer was working? (2) Wistaan's new metric takes fourteen days and is confounded by price, photographs and marketplace ranking. Is a slow, confounded metric pointing at the right outcome better than a fast, clean one pointing at the wrong outcome — and when would you reverse that judgement? (3) Warsha inverted the sign on Engagement. Name a surface in a product you know well where the sign is currently wrong, and the guardrail you would attach.

Section 13Going deeper

  1. What makes a good metric — sensitivity, validity and resistance to gaming: the layer underneath everything in Section 3.
  2. Vanity vs actionable metrics — the sharpest test of whether a selected category informs a decision or decorates a review; Warsha's engagement number is the canonical vanity case.
  3. GAME framework — an alternative selection scheme; comparing the two shows what HEART assumes about where goals come from.
  4. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — the business-outcome layer HEART is meant to lead; the join is what Wistaan was missing.
  5. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — formal vocabulary for the denominator arguments in Sections 3 and 6, including why ratio metrics misbehave in experiments.
  6. North Star metric — the rival position in Section 10's second disagreement; read it as a claim about attention, not a different chart.
  7. Attention, transaction, productivity games — a typology that predicts which HEART categories will matter, and which will mislead, before you have data.

Vistrit Care Cloud, Wistaan Studio, Vartul Market and Warsha Water Systems are fictional composites used for teaching.

UX Metrics: The HEART Framework

How do you measure the experience itself, and not just the business outcome it eventually produces?

1. A dashboard full of green, and a support queue full of complaints

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Meera Iyer, group product manager at Ginni Money, a Bengaluru-based personal finance app with eleven million registered users, sat in a review with her CEO holding two documents that told opposite stories. The first was the quarterly business dashboard: monthly transacting users up 9%, revenue from the premium subscription up 14%, churn flat. The second was a summary her support lead had prepared of six weeks of in-app feedback on Smart Budget, a redesigned expense-categorisation feature shipped in July. Users called it confusing; one-star reviews mentioned it by name. None of that showed up in the topline numbers.

The CEO's question was direct: is Smart Budget working or not? Meera did not have a good answer, because Ginni Money had never defined what "working" meant for a feature like this. Business metrics — revenue, transacting users, churn — were lagging and coarse; they would eventually reflect a bad experience, but only after enough users had already been frustrated, and only in a form that mixed Smart Budget's effect in with a dozen other things happening that quarter. Meera needed a way to measure the experience of using Smart Budget directly, this month, before it showed up as a dent in revenue three quarters later. That gap — between outcomes the business cares about and the experience that produces them — is exactly the problem the HEART framework was built to close.

2. The idea

HEART is a framework for choosing user-experience metrics, developed by Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson and Xin Fu, researchers on Google's user experience research team, and published in a 2010 paper titled "Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications." The letters stand for five categories of experience that matter to a product: Happiness (attitudes — satisfaction, perceived ease, willingness to recommend), Engagement (the level and depth of a user's involvement — frequency, intensity, breadth of feature use), Adoption (how many new or existing users start using a thing), Retention (whether users who started using it keep using it), and Task success (whether people can accomplish what they came to do — efficiency, effectiveness, error rate). Rodden and her colleagues were solving a specific problem: teams at Google kept defaulting to whichever metrics were easiest to log — usually clicks or page views — because there was no shared vocabulary for what else could be measured, and no discipline for picking metrics that matched what a feature was actually meant to do for the user.

The sentence Meera could repeat in a boardroom without sounding glib is this: HEART does not replace business metrics, it explains them, by giving each business outcome a small set of user-experience leading indicators that a team owns and can move in weeks rather than quarters. The framework's real discipline is not the five categories by themselves — most experienced PMs can list them from memory — but the requirement that follows: for each category you choose to use, you must state a Goal, a Signal, and a Metric, in that order, before you touch a dashboard. This is the Goals-Signals-Metrics, or GSM, process, and it is where HEART earns its keep.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in three deliberate steps, and the step practitioners most often skip is the first one: deciding which categories even apply. HEART is a menu, not a checklist — a feature aimed purely at completing a well-defined task (say, a KYC upload flow) may only need Task Success and Happiness; a feature meant to build a habit (a daily budgeting nudge) needs Engagement and Retention front and centre. Applying all five to every feature produces twenty metrics nobody owns and a dashboard nobody reads, which is precisely the failure mode HEART was invented to prevent.

Once Meera's team picked the relevant categories for Smart Budget — Happiness, Task Success, and Retention, with Engagement as a secondary watch — the GSM discipline required, for each one, first writing a Goal in plain language (what should be true if this category is healthy), then a Signal (an observable user behaviour or statement that would indicate the goal is or is not being met), and only then a Metric (the specific, computable number that operationalises the signal, with a defined population, window and formula). Skipping straight to metrics — "let's track categorisation completion rate" — without first writing the goal and signal is the single most common way teams end up measuring something precise but irrelevant. The goal keeps the metric honest; the signal is the bridge that keeps the metric traceable back to a real human behaviour rather than a convenient log event.

4. A worked example

Take Task Success, the category the CEO cared about most, since "confusing" was the word support kept hearing. Ginni Money's product analyst, Kabir Sethi, pulled four weeks of event logs for users who tapped a transaction to re-categorise it. Of 42,000 recategorisation attempts, 26,880 were completed in a single tap on the suggested alternative category, and the remaining 15,120 required the user to open a full category list and search. Task success rate, defined as single-tap completions divided by all attempts, was therefore 26,880 ÷ 42,000 = 64.0%. Median time-to-complete for the single-tap group was 6 seconds; for the search group it was 34 seconds. Combined with the CSAT data — an average of 3.4 out of 5 on the post-edit prompt, from 812 respondents that month — the numbers corroborated the complaints: a third of correction attempts were slow and effortful, and satisfaction sat below Ginni Money's 4.0 bar for a core flow.

Now run the second pass, changing one input: what if "success" is defined more strictly, as completing the correction and not repeating the same correction within seven days (a proxy for the category actually being fixed, not just re-tapped and abandoned)? Of the 26,880 single-tap completions, 3,360 saw the same transaction re-edited within a week — the suggested category had been accepted but was wrong again. Recomputing: (26,880 − 3,360) ÷ 42,000 = 56.0%. The eight-point drop matters enormously for what Meera does next: a 64% success rate suggests a UI friction problem (too many taps), while a 56% "durable success" rate that includes a persistent-error signal suggests the categorisation model itself is often wrong, which is an entirely different fix. This is the value of showing the arithmetic rather than asserting a conclusion: the same underlying data supports two different diagnoses depending on exactly how the metric is defined, which is why the Signal step in GSM — writing down, before you compute anything, what behaviour you are actually trying to detect — cannot be skipped.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Not every category applies to every feature

Forcing Adoption onto a feature that is on by default for all users, as Meera's team nearly did, produces a meaningless metric — there is no "adoption" to measure when there was no opt-in moment. HEART's categories are a menu you select from deliberately, not a form filled in out of habit.

Happiness metrics are attitudinal, and attitudes lag and lie

A CSAT score reflects how someone felt when asked, shaped by recency and mood. It is a real signal, but not a behavioural fact the way a completion rate is — users can rate a flow four stars out of politeness while quietly abandoning it.

Engagement is not automatically good

High engagement with a support-ticket flow, or an error-recovery screen, is a symptom of a problem, not evidence of health. The direction a metric should move only makes sense once you know what job the surface does for the user.

Retention needs a stated cohort and window before it means anything

"W4 retention" is meaningless without saying retention of whom, from what starting action, against what denominator — first-week triers, all active users, or paying subscribers tell different stories, and a bare percentage usually hides which one is meant.

Task success is easy to game by narrowing the task

Had Kabir defined success only as "reached the recategorisation screen," Smart Budget would have scored above 95%. A metric is only as honest as how faithfully the defined task matches what the user actually came to accomplish — the point of the second pass in Section 4.

HEART tells you where to look, not why

A falling Task Success rate tells Meera something is wrong with correction; it does not say whether the cause is the model, the copy, or a changed tap target. HEART metrics trigger qualitative follow-up — recordings, interviews — they do not replace it.

HEART metrics can conflict, and the conflict is informative

Engagement (more sessions correcting categories) can rise exactly when Task Success (fewer taps needed) is falling — more re-editing because the first attempt failed. Reading Engagement alone would have looked like good news.

A metric without an owner and a cadence decays into decoration

Every metric on a dashboard should state who is accountable for moving it and how often it is reviewed; one with neither is a chart nobody acts on.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and company stage

In a consumer app like Ginni Money, Happiness and Retention dominate because the relationship is high-frequency and self-serve, and small frictions compound across millions of sessions. In B2B products the picture shifts: a procurement platform like Hulchul Works, used by finance teams at mid-sized manufacturers, cares intensely about Task Success — did the purchase-order approval actually complete correctly — because a failed workflow can hold up a real payment, while Happiness is often measured through the account relationship (renewal conversations, account-level NPS) rather than in-app prompts, since individual users may lack the discretion to churn even if unhappy. Adoption in B2B is usually measured per seat within an account, because the buying decision and the using decision are made by different people.

Marketplaces split the picture further: a logistics marketplace like Lasya Freight runs HEART twice, once for shippers and once for fleet owners, because a metric healthy on one side (fast task completion for shippers posting a load) can coincide with one unhealthy on the other (drivers abandoning bids over unfair terms) — the business only works if both sides clear their bar. Early-stage companies lean on Happiness and Task Success while building the case the product works at all, with samples too small for stable retention curves; mature companies like Ginni Money lean harder on Retention and Engagement, since the core task is already proven and the question has shifted to whether habits form and last.

7. Common mistakes

The first mistake is metric-first thinking: a team picks a number because it is already instrumented, then invents a goal to justify it after the fact. The symptom is a dashboard where nobody can explain what decision a metric informs; the cheapest diagnostic is to ask each owner to state its Goal and Signal from memory — if they cannot, the GSM order was skipped.

The second is conflating Happiness with Retention, on the assumption that satisfied users obviously stay. Ginni Money had users who rated Smart Budget highly and still quietly stopped opening it, because satisfaction with one interaction and the durability of a habit are different phenomena; the diagnostic is to plot the two by cohort and look for divergence.

The third is a single global HEART scorecard for a multi-surface product, blending a healthy onboarding flow with a struggling core feature into one number that hides which surface needs attention; the fix is a HEART set per meaningful surface, not per app.

The fourth is treating a HEART metric as a target rather than an indicator — once a team is measured on Task Success, it redefines "task" more narrowly until the number rises without the experience improving, the classic Goodhart's-law failure; the diagnostic is to periodically re-derive the metric from its original Goal statement.

8. What good looks like

Three weeks after the review, Meera's team had a Smart Budget scorecard with three metrics, each with a named owner, a weekly cadence, and a written goal statement above it so nobody could forget what the number was for. Kabir owned Task Success, tracking both definitions from Section 4 so friction and model-accuracy problems could be told apart. The design lead owned Happiness, tied to a redesigned in-context prompt rather than a generic store rating. A data scientist owned four-week Retention, cohorted strictly by first-Budget-tab-use date. When the categorisation model was retrained in October using repeat-edit data as a labelled error set, durable Task Success moved from 56% to 71% in five weeks, CSAT rose to 4.1, and support tickets mentioning Smart Budget fell by half — and this time the CEO could see, in near real time, that the fix was working, rather than waiting two quarters for it to show in churn.

Meera's rule of thumb going forward: no feature ships without someone having written its Goal, Signal and Metric before the first line of instrumentation code — because a dashboard built after the fact always measures what was easy, not what mattered.

9. Closing

Meera's decision was not to add more dashboards but to narrow Smart Budget to three owned, goal-anchored metrics and retire the six vanity charts the team had accumulated since launch. The reasoning: a business metric like revenue would eventually have told the same story, but only after the damage was done and diluted with noise from everything else happening in the app; HEART, applied with real GSM discipline, gave her a leading, feature-specific, and diagnosable view weeks earlier. The natural next thing for a reader to study is the broader discipline of what makes a metric good in the first place — the properties (sensitivity, validity, resistance to gaming) that determined why "single-tap completion" was a defensible Task Success metric and "reached the screen" was not — since HEART only tells you which five doors to look behind, not how to judge what you find there. Two questions worth sitting with: when your own product's Happiness and Retention numbers move in opposite directions, which one should change your roadmap first, and why? And for a feature you know well, could you write its Goal, Signal and Metric from memory, in that order, right now — or would you, like Ginni Money before September, be reaching for whichever number was already on the dashboard?

Padhai Point: What Counts as a Good Doubt Corner

Jaipur, September 2026. Engagement is up, the rating is down, and a product manager has thirteen days to say what success means.

1. Thirteen days

On the morning of Thursday, 17 September 2026, Shruti Rao walked into Padhai Point's office on Tonk Road in Jaipur carrying a printout she had made at home because she did not trust herself to read it on a phone. It was a list of 1,840 Play Store reviews from the previous eight weeks, coded by theme by an intern in Bengaluru. Two thirds of the negative ones said some version of the same thing: maine doubt poocha, koi jawab nahin aaya — I asked a doubt, no answer came.

Shruti was senior product manager for Padhai Point's learning experience, and Doubt Corner was hers. It had launched on 14 June, in time for the SSC CGL preparation season, and by every number in the weekly growth review it had been the most successful thing the company shipped in two years. Daily actives were up 11 per cent, minutes per active user up 14 per cent, and Pro Batch conversions up 6 per cent. The chief executive, Nitin Gera, had put those three figures on the second slide of the Series C pre-read that went to investors in Mumbai and Singapore.

The roadmap for the Diwali quarter locked on 30 September. Doubt Corner V2 was in it, with four engineers from Pune assigned. What was not in it was any agreement on what V2 was supposed to improve. Nitin had asked Shruti, in a five-minute corridor conversation on Tuesday, for "the number that tells us Doubt Corner is working — and not a research project, Shruti, a number." She had thirteen days.

2. Padhai Point

Padhai Point was founded in 2017 by two former bank-exam coaching teachers from Kota who had recorded their classes on a ₹ 14,000 camera and put them on YouTube. By FY26 it had 2.6 crore registered learners, 19 lakh monthly actives and ₹ 104 crore of revenue, of which 78 per cent came from the Pro Batch subscription at ₹ 2,499 a year, sold almost entirely through UPI on Razorpay, and the rest from a white-label licensing business.

Its learners were preparing for government jobs: SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB NTPC, and eleven state police and revenue examinations. The median learner was 23, lived in a district town in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan or Madhya Pradesh, studied on an Android phone costing under ₹ 12,000, and had attempted at least one examination before. Padhai Point competed with Adda247 and Testbook for the same aspirants, and against Unacademy and PhysicsWallah for their attention and for teacher talent; the free tier competed, as everyone in Indian edtech competed, with YouTube.

The company had grown by being disciplined about one thing: content volume in Hindi. It had been much less disciplined about measurement. Its analytics stack was a standard event pipeline with a warehouse on top, and its product reviews ran on three numbers — daily actives, minutes, and Pro conversions — for every feature, regardless of what the feature did.

3. The situation

Doubt Corner let a learner photograph a question and post it. A mentor — one of 620 part-time subject experts, most of them graduate students paid ₹ 22 per accepted answer — would answer it. Other learners could upvote answers, and answered doubts appeared in a browsable feed organised by subject.

The browsable feed was the reason the engagement numbers looked good. Learners spent a great deal of time reading other people's doubts. What they were not reliably getting was answers to their own. In the first ninety days, 41.2 lakh doubts were posted and 15.6 lakh were answered — 38 per cent — with a median time to answer of 19 hours for those that were answered at all. Quantitative aptitude did reasonably well; Hindi-medium general-awareness questions about state-level current affairs did very badly, because Padhai Point had only 34 mentors who could handle them.

Her colleagues saw the situation from four different places, and the places mattered. Devansh Kulkarni's engineering team in Pune had built exactly what the specification asked for and had instrumented exactly the three metrics the company always asked for; adding an event for "asker marked this answer helpful" was two days of work that nobody had requested. Lena Kirchner, the product designer in Berlin, had run nine remote sessions with learners in Gorakhpur and Kota in August, staying up until one in the morning Central European Time to catch them after their evening study block, and had come away convinced that the experience was not slow — it was silent. Learners did not know whether a doubt had been seen. Rohit Menon, the data scientist in Toronto, had written to Shruti in August: "Minutes are up because the feed is sticky. That is a different product from the one the specification describes. I can't tell you whether asking works, because we don't log whether the asker got what they needed." And Grace Tan in Singapore had a commercial problem: Gulf Vidya Academy, a Dubai coaching chain that licensed Padhai Point's platform for ₹ 6.2 crore a year for its Indian-curriculum students, had escalated twice in September. Its academic head wanted a service level on doubt resolution, and Padhai Point had no metric with which to write one.

4. The people

The disagreement was not about facts. Everyone accepted the 38 per cent figure. The disagreement was about what Doubt Corner was for, and therefore about which number should decide whether it was working.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 contains the whole argument in two blocks. The top four rows are the numbers the company already watched, and they are all good. The middle rows are the numbers nobody had been watching, and the most consequential pair sits at the bottom of them: learners whose first doubt was answered came back to ask again 61 per cent of the time; learners whose doubt was ignored came back 9 per cent of the time. That is a seven-fold difference in behaviour attributable entirely to whether the product did the one thing it promised. The last row is the market's verdict, arriving with a lag.

Exhibit 3 is the constraint that makes this a real decision rather than a debate. Doubt Corner's gross cost today is ₹ 1.32 crore a month against a business generating roughly ₹ 9 crore a month in subscription revenue. Answering everything would nearly triple that cost. The middle row matters because it separates two things Shruti had been conflating: answering more doubts, which is expensive, and ending the silence, which is mostly a product change.

6. The options

Option A — keep the three numbers and ship the growth version

V2 as currently specified in the Pune backlog: push notifications when a doubt in your subject is answered, a daily "doubt streak", and unanswered doubts surfaced in the feed so the community can answer them. It ships on 12 October, costs nothing beyond the engineers already assigned, and will almost certainly raise daily actives and minutes further. Nitin's slide keeps improving. Nothing in this option changes the probability that Shruti's own learner gets an answer, and Exhibit 2 suggests the notification volume will add to a complaint category that is already at 9 per cent.

Option B — build the full measurement programme first

Instrument all five dimensions of the learning experience: a quarterly sampled survey run by Lena's team in Hindi and English, new events for every step of the ask-and-answer flow, adoption and retention cohorts by subject, and a mentor-side dashboard. Rohit has scoped it at ₹ 42 lakh — largely a research vendor and two months of a contract analytics engineer — plus six weeks of Devansh's team, which pushes V2 past Diwali into January. It would give Padhai Point a measurement system it does not have. It would also mean the worst quarter for answer rates passes uninstrumented and the Gulf Vidya renewal arrives with no metric attached.

Option C — two metrics tied to the promise, shipped in three weeks

Define success as a pair. First, resolution rate: the share of posted doubts that receive an answer the asker then marks helpful, within 24 hours — two new events, three days of Devansh's time. Second, a three-question in-product micro-survey shown to 1 in 10 askers 48 hours after posting, asking whether they got what they needed, whether the answer was clear, and whether they would ask again. Daily actives and minutes stay on the dashboard as guardrails with no target. V2's scope changes: instead of streaks and notifications, it builds visible routing — an acknowledgement within thirty minutes, a stated queue, and an honest refusal for subjects with no mentor coverage — which Exhibit 3 costs at roughly ₹ 74 lakh a month more if paired with a move to a 60 per cent answer rate, or almost nothing if shipped alone as transparency. Ships 8 October. Gives Grace a number for Dubai. Does not give Nitin a bigger slide.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 1 shows engagement, revenue and rating moving in different directions at the same time. What is the most plausible single explanation that accounts for all three, and what in the exhibit would you want to check before accepting it?

2. Padhai Point evaluates every feature on daily actives, minutes and conversions. For Doubt Corner specifically, what does each of those three numbers actually measure, and what does none of them measure?

3. Grace Tan needs a metric she can write into the Gulf Vidya renewal as a service level. Which of the candidate metrics in this case could survive being contractual, and what would each of them do to the behaviour of Padhai Point's mentor operations team once money depended on it?

4. It is 30 September. Which option do you choose, what exactly do you put in the roadmap document, and what do you say to Nitin about the Series C slide?

8. A note for the learner

This case is an argument about measuring the experience rather than the outcome. Padhai Point's three standing numbers — actives, minutes, conversions — are business and engagement metrics. They are not wrong, and they are not enough: a feature can raise all three while failing at the only job it was built to do. The HEART framework exists for exactly this gap, naming five kinds of experience evidence: happiness, engagement, adoption, retention and task success. Its discipline is not to fill in all five boxes but to choose the ones the goal depends on, and to say out loud which ones you are not measuring and why.

The method behind the framework is to move from goal to signal to metric. Doubt Corner's goal, written in the learner's words, is "I get a clear answer to my question quickly enough to keep studying tonight." The signal that this happened is an answer the asker accepts, arriving the same evening. The metric is a resolution rate with a time bound and an asker's judgement in it. Run the same descent on happiness and you get a short survey of askers, not a general app-satisfaction score — Exhibit 2 shows how a general rating buries the specific defect among crashes and notifications. Run it on engagement and you find that minutes per active user measures the browsable feed, which is a different product; that makes engagement a useful guardrail and a dangerous target. Adoption is not in question, since 41.2 lakh doubts were posted. Retention shows up in the most striking line in Exhibit 1, the 61-versus-9 per cent gap, which is a retention consequence of a task-success failure.

A well-reasoned answer therefore does three things: it names the two or three categories that bear on the goal and justifies the omissions; it attaches an owner, a cadence and a decision to each metric it keeps; and it treats Exhibit 3 as a constraint on the choice rather than a separate problem.

One defensible path. Choose Option C, and change V2's scope to visible routing rather than streaks. The reasoning runs as follows. The goal is task success, and the case contains direct evidence that task success drives the business outcome Nitin cares about — the 61-versus-9 per cent repeat-ask gap, and a rating decline whose complaints are 56 per cent about the missing answer. Option A optimises a metric that is already saturating the wrong behaviour and adds to a live complaint category. Option B is right about the destination and wrong about the timing: it spends the Diwali quarter, when evidence is cheapest and the answer rate worst, building instruments rather than using them, and it arrives after the Dubai renewal conversation. Option C buys the two metrics that matter for three days of engineering, gives Grace a contractual candidate, and separates the expensive question (answer more doubts, ₹ 74 lakh a month) from the cheap one (stop being silent). Shruti keeps minutes and actives on the dashboard without targets, and offers Nitin a different slide: resolution rate as the number that goes up, with the repeat-ask gap as the reason investors should believe it leads revenue.

What would change this answer? If the repeat-ask gap turned out to be selection rather than causation — if answered doubts were simply the easier doubts asked by more committed learners — the causal claim weakens and Option B's insistence on proper instrumentation looks wiser. And if Gulf Vidya's renewal were worth ₹ 25 crore rather than ₹ 6.2 crore, the case for spending on the 95 per cent answer rate would be commercial rather than pedagogical.
